items.title: Andrej Karpathy says understanding of large language model capabilities is diverging sharply among different user groups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening
items.summary:
Andrej Karpathy highlights a widening gap in shared understanding of large language model (LLM) capabilities, noting that about 75% of the global population has little to no interaction with LLMs, while a small fraction of professionals experience advanced, frontier-grade applications. He categorizes users into groups ranging from casual users who see LLMs as simple chatbots to a tiny elite using cutting-edge systems for complex tasks like software development and scientific research.
Karpathy explains this divergence is driven by factors including the scale of problems tackled, domain-specific capability peaks in areas like math and coding, and varying levels of access to LLM technology. He emphasizes that while most people see only modest improvements, a small group is witnessing rapid, transformative impacts, creating a sharp funnel of understanding and experience with AI capabilities.

items.title: Sakana AI researchers introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS) for recursive self-improvement using collective intelligence in AI models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence
items.summary:
Researchers at Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have developed Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), a method enabling AI models to recursively improve themselves by optimizing multi-agent workflows and distilling collective intelligence as a self-supervision signal. MASS uses a single language model to act as executor, optimizer, and evaluator, iteratively refining team workflows and learning from self-judged best executions to enhance performance on non-verifiable research tasks.

The approach draws inspiration from human collective learning and scientific communities, where shared knowledge and division of labor drive progress. MASS's recursive loop involves the model optimizing its own workflows and evaluating results without external supervision, with progress measured by independent assessments from GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. This method aims to advance AI beyond current human knowledge by enabling continual self-learning where the model is both the optimizer and evaluator.

items.title: Researchers introduce SpireBench to evaluate long-horizon strategic play of large language models using the game Slay the Spire [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SpireBench, a benchmark that tests the long-term strategic reasoning of large language models (LLMs) by having them play the full commercial deck-building game Slay the Spire at its highest difficulty. The study evaluated 20 LLMs, finding that while advanced models outperform heuristic baselines and match average human players, they still fall short of expert-level performance, especially as game length increases. Models tend to misjudge risk and rely on prior knowledge rather than learning from past runs, limiting their strategic adaptation.

SpireBench provides a comprehensive framework to analyze where and why agentic models fail in extended strategic tasks, offering tools to dissect performance across different game stages and highlighting challenges in risk assessment and memory utilization. This benchmark is the first to give models access to the complete original game, enabling a detailed comparison with existing evaluation methods and advancing the study of long-horizon strategic reasoning in AI.

items.title: Researchers introduce VEPA, a verified evolving formal policy framework for deterministic lifelong guardrails in large language model agents interacting with sensitive resources [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
items.summary:
Researchers have developed VEPA, a framework that enforces deterministic, inspectable guardrails for large language model (LLM) agents operating over sensitive data and mutable system states. VEPA uses executable symbolic rules as formal policies and adapts these policies during deployment by proposing verified updates guided by LLM feedback, ensuring conflict-free and evidence-supported rule activation to maintain safety and security.

VEPA addresses limitations of existing adaptive guardrails that rely on LLM inference and can produce inconsistent decisions by combining formal verification with adaptive policy evolution. Evaluations on multiple benchmarks show VEPA outperforms baseline methods, maintaining effectiveness even under challenging conditions such as mixed data streams, corrupted feedback, and extended deployment horizons.

items.originalSummary: Researchers have introduced VEPA, a new framework designed to enhance the safety and security of large language model (LLM) agents that interact with sensitive resources. VEPA employs a formal policy system with executable symbolic rules to enforce deterministic guardrails, ensuring consistent and inspectable decisions before agent actions are executed. Unlike existing adaptive guardrails that rely on LLM inference and may produce inconsistent outcomes, VEPA uses deployment feedback guided by an LLM to propose policy updates, which are then verified for validity and conflict-free status before activation. An evidence-aware authority layer further ensures that only rules supported by sufficient evidence influence decisions. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that VEPA outperforms existing methods, maintaining effectiveness even under challenging deployment scenarios such as mixed data streams and corrupted feedback.

items.title: Researchers develop a multi-agent LLM system for automated tuning of specialized neural network components, improving performance across spiking neural networks and physics-informed neural networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
items.summary: Researchers propose a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework with distinct analyst, coder, and recorder roles to automate tuning of key components in specialized neural networks without altering overall architecture. The system operates in a semantically narrow code generation space and is validated on tasks including spiking neural network classification and solving differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). The approach outperforms baselines by significant margins, achieving up to 13 percentage points higher classification accuracy on MNIST and reducing error metrics by several orders of magnitude in physics-based tasks. This framework demonstrates transferable automated tuning across diverse neural network models while maintaining internal structure.

The approach outperforms baselines by significant margins, achieving up to 13 percentage points higher classification accuracy on MNIST and reducing error metrics by several orders of magnitude in physics-based tasks. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

items.title: Adaptive DHiSparse supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV with load-adaptive residency, improving throughput and concurrency in long-context serving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
items.summary:
Adaptive DHiSparse is a new system designed to enhance long-context serving by supporting speculative decoding over a hierarchical sparse key-value (KV) memory structure that adapts residency based on load. It protects essential working sets, retains additional history when GPU memory is available, and recovers remaining data through exact fused retrieval, improving efficiency over previous methods like HiSparse, DSpark, and DFlash2.

In tests with GLM-5.3 at 100K context and concurrency 128, Adaptive DHiSparse with DFlash2 achieved 793 output tokens per second per decode GPU, outperforming HiSparse by 1.45 times and non-speculative adaptive serving by 1.27 times. It also sustained up to four times the concurrency and increased output by 2.3 to 3.7 times under the same latency constraints. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, it delivered 1.85 times the output of resident serving with DSpark. Additionally, optional residency management reduced host fetches significantly at low load and freed memory under pressure.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.

items.originalTitle: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers investigate on-policy self-distillation, where a teacher model scores a student's rollout to provide token-level credit for reinforcement learning, and find that traditional scoring signals fail to localize errors or distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning traces. They identify this limitation as structural, since error localization requires a search process that scoring alone does not perform. To address this, they introduce critique-conditioned self-distillation, where the teacher first generates a critique of the rollout and then conditions its scoring on that critique, resulting in better error localization and corrective feedback that encourages backtracking tokens like "Wait" and "But." This approach improves model performance on math problems at test time and provides useful signals in cold-start reinforcement learning scenarios where verifiable rewards are sparse.
items.description: Researchers investigate on-policy self-distillation, where a teacher model scores a student's rollout to provide token-level credit for reinforcement learning, and find that traditional scoring signals fail to localize errors or distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning traces. They identify this limitation as structural, since error localization requires a search process that scoring alone does not perform. To address this, they introduce critique-conditioned self-distillation, where the teacher first generates a critique of the rollout and then conditions its scoring on that critique, resulting in better error localization and corrective feedback that encourages backtracking tokens like "Wait" and "But." This approach improves model performance on math problems at test time and provides useful signals in cold-start reinforcement learning scenarios where verifiable rewards are sparse.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.

items.title: Kairos introduces a byte-level foundation model combining novel attention mechanisms and a multi-scale codec for multimodal data, with initial optimization tests on text [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
items.summary: Kairos presents a foundation model designed to process multiple data modalities at the byte level, integrating bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention, sliding-window attention, block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts feed-forward layer, and a multi-scale byte-level codec. The model is trained using a uniform-noise denoising objective over a shared byte space encompassing text, image, audio, video, lidar, and control streams. Initial experiments focus on convergence and optimization using text-only data, specifically overfitting a single 440-byte sentence with parameter counts ranging from 1 to 15 million.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .

items.title: AutoIndexer introduces flexible-order decoding by training causal models on chains of edits to enable post-generation token insertions, substitutions, and deletions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
items.summary: AutoIndexer is a generative model designed to overcome limitations of autoregressive decoding in handling non-causally ordered data by simulating a chain of edits that allows flexible modifications of prior outputs through token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model predicts marker tokens to open and close edits and moves a cursor within the token sequence, similar to a text editor, enabling it to revise outputs post hoc. Training involves perturbing ground-truth sequences with inverse chained edits, teaching the model to undo these perturbations, which enhances robustness to erroneous context and adaptability to tasks like code correction. The method demonstrates post-generation editing capabilities absent in most autoregressive and diffusion models without sacrificing performance on standard language model benchmarks, with code available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.

items.title: Researchers propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that uses backward revision to improve online adaptation in language model agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning
items.summary: Researchers introduce ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework designed to enhance continual learning in language model agents by incorporating backward revision alongside forward read and write under an online streaming protocol. This approach revises reflections based on feedback from each interaction, aiming to better capture information and adapt to distribution shifts without relying on replay or validation data. Across multiple benchmarks and language model backbones, ReHarness outperforms existing methods including raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based techniques, and prompt optimization. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces meaningful, source-grounded revisions, corrects outdated experiences, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.

Across multiple benchmarks and language model backbones, ReHarness outperforms existing methods including raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based techniques, and prompt optimization. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents increasingly operate over long interaction streams, requiring online adaptation to distribution shifts through continual learning. However, existing agent harnesses typically either evolve their states only through forward information flow or rely on additional replay or validation data for harness optimization. To address this, we propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that complements forward read and write with backward revision under a strictly online streaming protocol. We ask what information could have been captured differently in the harness state to better inform the current instance in the stream. Specifically, after each instance, we leverage the resulting trajectory as feedback to revise the reflections retrieved for that instance, thereby propagating feedback backward through the textual harness state. Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms strong raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces source-grounded and meaningful revisions, corrects overgeneralized or outdated experience under distribution shifts, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.

items.title: Researchers propose REDaCT, an inference-time unlearning framework for large reasoning models that prevents reasoning collapse while removing forget-set information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: REDaCT: Collapse-Free Unlearning in Large Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce REDaCT (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning), a new method for unlearning in large reasoning models that avoids reasoning collapse by detecting and correcting sentences leaking forget-set information during inference. REDaCT uses a binary leak detector and an embedding optimization module to guide reasoning away from leaked information, maintaining coherent chain-of-thought and proper reasoning termination.

Experimental results demonstrate that REDaCT outperforms existing unlearning methods by preserving reasoning quality while achieving perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect chain-of-thought forgetting. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further study and application.
items.description:
Researchers introduce REDaCT (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning), a new method for unlearning in large reasoning models that avoids reasoning collapse by detecting and correcting sentences leaking forget-set information during inference. REDaCT uses a binary leak detector and an embedding optimization module to guide reasoning away from leaked information, maintaining coherent chain-of-thought and proper reasoning termination.

Experimental results demonstrate that REDaCT outperforms existing unlearning methods by preserving reasoning quality while achieving perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect chain-of-thought forgetting. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further study and application.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unlearning in large reasoning models (LRMs) requires removing forget-set information from both the reasoning trace and the final answer. Existing approaches achieve this objective at the cost of reasoning collapse, where the model fails to produce a coherent chain-of-thought (CoT) and does not properly terminate its reasoning process. To address this challenge, we propose REDaCT (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning), an inference-time unlearning framework for LRMs. REDaCT consists of two key components: (1) a binary leak detector that identifies sentences in the reasoning trace that leak forget-set information, and (2) an embedding optimization module that learns a corrective embedding offline, such that when injected at the first detected leak during inference, it guides subsequent reasoning towards sentences that do not leak forget-set information. Experimental results show that REDaCT completely avoids reasoning collapse, substantially improving reasoning preservation compared to state-of-the-art unlearning methods while maintaining perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect CoT forgetting. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jmaccoby/redact.

items.title: Researchers introduce CoCoEvolve, a meta-reflective evolutionary optimizer that improves production AI systems across data agents, LLM data pipelines, and data engineering workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems
items.summary: Researchers present CoCoEvolve, an evolutionary optimizer using meta-reflection to improve production AI systems by selectively retrieving evidence from evolutionary history and probing live systems before proposing mutations. CoCoEvolve outperforms existing methods on benchmarks including DABStep, data-eng-bench, and HotpotQA, achieving higher accuracy and solve rates than prior baselines. The approach demonstrates the value of meta-reflection in optimizing complex AI workflows beyond traditional frontier-focused mutation methods.

CoCoEvolve outperforms existing methods on benchmarks including DABStep, data-eng-bench, and HotpotQA, achieving higher accuracy and solve rates than prior baselines. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-guided evolutionary optimization has successfully improved prompts, programs, and even entire AI systems. Most optimization methods select a candidate from the search frontier, then mutate it in one LLM pass based only on its failures. This focus on the frontier can stall on production AI systems, where isolated failures reveal little about complex, hidden interactions. We introduce CoCoEvolve (Cortex Code Evolve), an evolutionary optimizer built around what we call meta-reflection, wherein an agentic mutator (Cortex Code) selectively retrieves evidence from the entire evolutionary history and probes the live system before verifying and proposing mutations. We apply CoCoEvolve to optimize three classes of production AI systems: data agents, LLM-powered data pipelines, and data engineering workflows. On DABStep, CoCoEvolve tops the public leaderboard, reaching 92.8% held-out hard accuracy compared to 78.4% for Meta-Harness and 30.4% for GEPA under matched conditions. Across six LLM data pipeline workloads, it outperforms every evaluated baseline. On data-eng-bench, CoCoEvolve lifts test-set solve rate from 59.1% to 77.4%, past the best baseline of 73.6%. It also has 11 percentage points higher accuracy than GEPA on HotpotQA while remaining competitive with specialized optimizers on established mathematical and systems benchmarks. Matched ablations confirm that each component of CoCoEvolve contributes to these gains, demonstrating the value of meta-reflection for optimizing production AI systems.

items.title: COFFEQA introduces counterfactual-guided few-shot distillation to improve LLM question answering accuracy using validated factual-counterfactual pairs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
items.summary:
COFFEQA is a new method for knowledge distillation that trains smaller student models to mimic larger teacher models in question answering tasks using limited training samples. It leverages counterfactual examples—minimally modified contexts that change the teacher's answer—to provide additional supervision and improve distillation performance, addressing issues caused by uncertain samples near decision boundaries. The approach introduces a metric called Context Following Difficulty (CFD) to validate counterfactuals before distillation.

Experiments on multiple in-domain and out-of-domain QA benchmarks with T5 and Qwen2.5 models show that COFFEQA outperforms traditional factual-only few-shot distillation methods under the same sample budget. For example, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves exact match and F1 scores by approximately 8.77 and 9.98 points respectively using 32 few-shot pairs with the T5 model.

This work provides geometric insights into how factual-counterfactual pairs constrain the divergence between teacher and student decision boundaries, offering a more efficient and effective distillation strategy for generative question answering models in resource-constrained settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.

items.title: Researchers propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic supervised fine-tuning method that improves generalization in large language models without extra data or online rollouts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers introduce CIG-SFT, a supervised fine-tuning framework that estimates task-conditioned information gain for each demonstrated token to enhance post-training of large language models. This method compares token likelihoods from a frozen reference model with and without task input to quantify how much the task reduces uncertainty about decisions, then incorporates this into a KL-regularized projection for fine-tuning.

CIG-SFT outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning and recent adaptive methods on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, showing stronger generalization to challenging evaluation distributions. The approach achieves these improvements without requiring additional training data or online rollouts, addressing limitations of forcing models to imitate fixed demonstrations that may interfere with pretrained behaviors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.

items.title: Researchers introduce CoBe benchmark to evaluate models' zero-shot conversational counterfactual text editing across 2000 scenarios in healthcare, science, business, and daily life [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
items.summary: Researchers have developed the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe) to test language models' ability to perform counterfactual text editing, which involves revising text based on hypothetical changes while preserving unaffected facts. CoBe includes 2000 questions spanning multiple domains and assesses models' zero-shot performance in conversational settings, revealing that current models often default to associational text generation rather than maintaining causal consistency. The study found that performance does not reliably improve with larger model size or longer outputs, suggesting limitations stem from training objectives rather than model capacity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counterfactual text editing is the ability to revise a given text in light of a hypothetical change while preserving facts not causally affected by that change. When asked what would have happened if a doctor had not recommended surgery, the model output should retain the patient's medical history and modify only the consequences of the decision. This requires causal understanding: a model must determine, without being explicitly instructed to, what events are affected by the hypothetical change and what should remain fixed. This skill is central to human reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare or law. By contrast, the task of associational text generation merely generates text statistically associated with the altered condition. In the medical example, an associational response might make the patient's symptoms less severe because milder cases correlate with no surgery. Such responses produce a plausible scenario, but not the counterfactual version of the given one. Prior counterfactual-text datasets do not clearly separate these modes of reasoning. We introduce the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe), a testbed for models' zero-shot ability to counterfactually edit a given textual scenario when prompted to do so in a conversationally natural way. CoBe contains 2000 questions spanning healthcare, science and engineering, business, and everyday scenarios. We test a suite of frontier and smaller models, with frontier systems achieving an average score of $58.05\%$. Our findings indicate that models frequently default to associational generation rather than preserving the causal structure of the original scenario. Moreover, performance does not scale consistently with either model size or output token length, suggesting that the failure may reflect model training objectives rather than insufficient model capacity.

items.title: Researchers introduce Agents' Last Exam benchmark to evaluate AI agents on long-term, economically valuable tasks across 13 industry clusters with over 1,000 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agents' Last Exam
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents on extended, economically significant real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Created with input from over 250 industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries based on the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy and includes 55 subfields grouped into 13 industry clusters encompassing more than 1,000 tasks. Current results indicate that the most challenging tasks remain largely unsolved, with an average full pass rate below 1% across standard configurations.

ALE is intended as a living benchmark that will expand continuously as new workflows and industries are added. Its goal is to bridge the gap between AI benchmark performance and meaningful economic impact, moving beyond traditional leaderboards to measure sustained performance on tasks relevant to GDP.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.05405v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent AI systems have achieved strong results on a wide range of benchmarks, yet these gains have not translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional domains. We argue that this gap is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks lack sustained performance measurement on real and economically valuable workflows. This paper introduces Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on long horizon, economically valuable, real world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed in collaboration with 250+ industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries defined with reference to O*NET / SOC 2018 (the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy). It is organized around a task taxonomy with 55 sub fields grouped into 13 industry clusters covering 1K+ tasks. Current results show that the hardest tier remains far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is below 1%. ALE is designed as a living benchmark: its task pool grows continuously as new workflows and industries are onboarded. More broadly, ALE is intended not merely as another leaderboard, but as an instrument for closing the gap between benchmark success and GDP relevant impact.

items.title: Researchers introduce an auditing framework that uses fine-tuning artifacts to reveal vulnerabilities in prompt injection defenses, raising attack success rates up to 96% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Prompt Injection Defenses Before They Reach Users: What Strong Adversaries Reveal
items.summary: Researchers have developed an auditing framework that stress-tests prompt injection defenses in large language models before deployment by leveraging intermediate fine-tuning checkpoints as stepping stones for optimization-based attacks. This approach exposes genuine vulnerabilities that realistic adversaries could exploit, significantly increasing attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses from near zero to as high as 96%. The study highlights that current evaluation methods may overestimate robustness and emphasizes the importance of rigorous pre-release testing to prevent real-world harm to users.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2505.15738v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in user-facing products that handle sensitive personal data while interacting with untrusted external content. This makes them a prime target for prompt injection attacks, in which an adversary injects malicious instructions in that content to hijack the model. Fine-tuning-based defenses have been proposed to mitigate these attacks by training models to follow benign user instructions and ignore injected ones. Lacking formal guarantees, these defenses are evaluated empirically against the most effective realistic attacks available at the time, often reporting near-zero attack success rates -- giving developers, and the users who depend on them, a false sense of security and leaving open the possibility that future, more capable attacks could circumvent them and cause severe consequences in widely deployed systems. In this paper, we argue that developers should stress-test their defenses before release, and we introduce an auditing framework that does so without requiring defenders to invent the next state-of-the-art attack. Our key insight is that the fine-tuning process itself yields useful artifacts: intermediate checkpoints that serve as stepping stones for optimization-based attacks. Although these artifacts are unavailable to real attackers, we show that the vulnerabilities they expose are genuine and can be exploited by realistic adversaries. Instantiating our framework with optimization-based attacks such as GCG and BEAST, we raise attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses from near zero to as high as 96\%, revealing weaknesses missed by prior evaluations. Our results show that current evaluation practices can substantially overestimate robustness, and that auditing defenses under strong adversaries before deployment shortens the feedback loop and helps prevent attacks from causing real-world harm to users.

items.title: Researchers audit six large language models for intersectional disability bias in 2,820 hiring scenarios using new ABLEIST metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ABLEIST: Intersectional Disability Bias in LLM-Generated Hiring Scenarios
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a comprehensive audit of six large language models (LLMs) across 2,820 hiring scenarios to evaluate bias against people with disabilities (PwD), focusing on intersectional factors such as gender and caste. They introduced ABLEIST, a set of metrics grounded in disability studies, to measure ableism and intersectional harms like tokenism and superhumanization in LLM outputs.

The study found significant increases in ableism-related harms toward disabled candidates that many state-of-the-art models failed to detect. These harms were further amplified for disabled candidates marginalized by gender and caste, revealing critical blind spots in current AI safety tools and underscoring the need for intersectional evaluations of LLMs in high-stakes domains like hiring.

items.summary: Researchers introduce COBALT, a method that reuses offline multi-turn code generation trajectories to efficiently train large language models (LLMs) without costly online reinforcement learning. COBALT treats multi-turn code generation as a one-step recoverable Markov decision process, training LLMs to complete partial code trajectories through single-step generation. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.03806v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) for multi-turn code generation typically relies on online reinforcement learning (RL), in which models learn from repeatedly generated online rollouts. Although effective, online RL can be costly and unstable. In this paper, we present contextual bandit learning with offline trajectories (COBALT), a simple method that reuses offline multi-turn trajectories to efficiently train LLMs for multi-turn code generation. Building on the observation that multi-turn code generation is a one-step recoverable Markov decision process, COBALT first collects code generation trajectories using a reference LLM and divides them into partial trajectories. Then, during online bandit learning, the LLM is trained to complete each partial trajectory through single-step code generation. On LiveCodeBench, COBALT substantially improves R1-Distill 8B and Qwen3 8B by up to 9.0 and 6.2 absolute Pass@1 points and matches the performance of two multi-turn online RL baselines using GRPO and VeRPO. We also perform a perturbation-based analysis of in-context reward hacking and show that Cobalt can improve robustness to misleading execution feedback. Overall, our results demonstrate that Cobalt is a promising solution for multi-turn code generation. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/cobalt.

items.title: Researchers propose PACT, a Privileged Trace Co-Training framework to improve multi-turn tool-use agents by combining reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning with expert trace optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PACT: Privileged Trace Co-Training for Multi-Turn Tool-Use Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce PACT, a training framework designed to enhance multi-turn tool-use agents that must reason, call tools, and adapt over multiple interaction turns. PACT uses expert traces only during training as optimization signals rather than during rollout, combining a trace-conditioned reinforcement learning surrogate and a component-aware supervised fine-tuning loss to guide learning while maintaining prompt-only rollout generation.

Experiments on benchmarks including FTRL, BFCL, and ToolHop demonstrate that PACT outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines. The approach reduces over-reliance on training-only trace context by incorporating prompt-only anchoring and standard reinforcement learning updates, highlighting the benefits of privileged trace co-training for multi-turn tool-use learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.16215v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-turn tool-use agents must reason, call tools, and adapt to observations across several interaction turns. Post-training such agents is challenging, as reinforcement learning often suffers from sparse rewards and weak credit assignment despite matching the prompt-only inference setting, while supervised fine-tuning on expert traces provides dense process supervision but can over-constrain the model to fixed trajectories. To tackle this, we propose PACT, a Privileged trAce Co-Training framework for multi-turn tool-use agents. The key idea is to use expert traces only as training-time optimization signals rather than rollout-time hints. PACT keeps rollout generation prompt-only, then uses expert traces to guide optimization through two complementary signals: a trace-conditioned RL surrogate that evaluates prompt-only rollouts under expert-trace context, and a component-aware SFT loss that provides annealed process supervision over reasoning and tool-call components. To reduce over-reliance on the training-only trace context, PACT incorporates prompt-only anchoring with standard prompt-only RL updates. Experiments on FTRL, BFCL, and ToolHop show that PACT consistently outperforms strong SFT- and RL-based baselines. Further analyses support the complementarity of the two training objectives and the benefits of component-aware supervision and prompt-only anchoring. These results highlight the effectiveness of privileged trace co-training for multi-turn tool-use learning. The project page is available at https://zhenbangdu.github.io/pact-project-page.

items.title: Study finds medical foundation models trained with label supervision converge less in image representation across modalities and datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Medical foundation models converge less under label supervision
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated over 750,000 medical images from 14 datasets and 5 imaging modalities using 119 models to assess how similarly different medical foundation models represent images. They measured agreement by the overlap of nearest neighbors in model embeddings and found that models trained with label supervision showed the least convergence, especially in chest radiography and histopathology, compared to models trained with self-distillation, masked image modeling, or contrastive pretraining. Agreement depended more on dataset source and imaging view than on diagnostic findings and was not strongly linked to accuracy.

The study also demonstrated that a linear mapping between embeddings of two models could transfer classifiers for multiple chest findings with high accuracy, suggesting practical interoperability despite differences in model representations. The findings imply that developers can influence model convergence through pretraining objectives, and users might test successor models on unlabeled images to verify consistency before replacement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.20274v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diagnostic classifiers and imaging biomarkers are fitted on the embeddings of medical foundation models. These models are replaced as new versions appear. This practice assumes that different models represent images alike. We tested this assumption with more than 750,000 images from 14 datasets in 5 imaging modalities, 18 public models, and 101 models trained on chest radiographs and histopathology that differ in pretraining objective, label type, size, random seed, initialization, training patients, or training recipe. Agreement was measured as the mutual k-nearest-neighbor overlap, the share of an image's nearest neighbors common to two models. Two public models shared on average 0.091 of the 10 nearest neighbors of a chest radiograph. A randomly initialized network shared 0.036 with them. In the four other modalities, they shared at most 0.300. On chest radiographs, agreement depended more on the source dataset and the radiographic view than on the findings. It was not significantly associated with accuracy. A linear mapping between the embeddings of two models, fitted on 4,096 unlabeled radiographs, transferred classifiers for 14 chest findings with 0.987 of their original area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Convergence depended on the pretraining objective. Label-supervised models converged least at both model sizes in chest radiography and histopathology. On chest radiographs, two label-supervised models that differed only in their random seed shared 0.062 to 0.100 of their nearest neighbors. Two models trained with self-distillation, masked image modeling, or contrastive pretraining shared 0.411 to 0.802. Developers can therefore choose convergence when they choose the pretraining objective. Before replacing a model, users could test on unlabeled images whether its successor returns the same nearest neighbors.

items.title: OpenCollab launches a multi-agent coding framework with programmable collaboration and controllable runtime, achieving up to 97.2% adherence and new state-of-the-art performance in benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
items.summary:
OpenCollab introduces a unified multi-agent coding framework designed to improve collaboration in complex software engineering tasks by providing programmable collaboration and a controllable runtime environment. The framework enforces experimental control, tracks execution through detailed event streams, and quantifies adherence to declared organizational structures, revealing significant variation in agent collaboration across configurations.

Experiments show that OpenCollab's Duo configuration outperforms existing multi-agent coding systems such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, while its single-agent setup uses fewer tokens across evaluated benchmarks. This framework establishes a controlled infrastructure for programmable collaboration and causal evaluation in multi-agent coding systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2609.38345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration and controlled causal evaluation.

items.title: Position paper outlines five key shortcomings of current Explainable AI faithfulness metrics for feature importance and proposes four research directions to improve their reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
items.summary:
A recent position paper examines the limitations of faithfulness metrics used to evaluate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods that provide feature importance explanations. The authors argue that while XAI aims to build trust by making machine learning models more interpretable, current approaches often oversimplify model behavior, leading to unfaithful explanations that do not accurately reflect the model's decision process. The paper identifies five major structural misalignments in existing faithfulness metrics, which make rigorous quantification of explanation trustworthiness computationally expensive or infeasible.

The authors propose four avenues for future research to address these shortcomings and enhance the reliability of faithfulness measurements. They emphasize that improving these metrics is crucial for advancing the trustworthiness and practical utility of XAI tools, which currently function more effectively as debugging aids than as definitive explanations for model predictions.

items.title: Study finds Monte Carlo Tree Search underperforms randomized-restart list scheduling by 2.88% on DAG workflow scheduling with equal computational budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
items.summary: A controlled study compared Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling methods for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows using identical computational budgets. At a budget of 2048 evaluated schedules, MCTS performed about 2.88% worse than randomized restarts, with the performance gap not attributable to insufficient budget. The study tested workflows with up to 32 tasks and 8 processors in synthetic domains, finding that restarts outperformed MCTS on sparse irregular workflows, while no significant difference appeared on regular layered workflows and dense workflows showed limited room for improvement. Using a textbook UCT selection rule reduced MCTS's deficit but did not reverse it. The results do not extend claims to larger-scale or higher-budget scenarios.

items.title: Researchers develop MagicBeanStalk, a recursive data synthesis algorithm to improve reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning by generating balanced, challenging training problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MagicBeanStalk, an algorithm that generates training problems calibrated to a target policy and training budget to enhance reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning (RLVR). They identified that existing large math problem datasets often fall into a 'zero-advantage trap,' where most problems are either always solved or always failed, limiting learning effectiveness. MagicBeanStalk overcomes this by recursively expanding seed problems into diverse families that preserve reasoning structures while maintaining balanced difficulty.

Experiments on eight math benchmarks showed that training on MagicBeanStalk problems significantly improved model performance compared to existing datasets, with gains of 8.6 points for gpt-oss-120b and 5.4 points for DeepSeek v4Flash on a 16K-token budget. The approach was also applied in finance, synthesizing over 14,000 verifiable problems from 340 solutions and achieving notable improvements on financial reasoning benchmarks SecQue and FinanceBench.

items.title: Researchers introduce SmartSalesBench, a multi-turn benchmark evaluating LLM sales agents against resistant buyer personas across 13,680 sessions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
items.summary: SmartSalesBench is a new benchmark designed to test large language model (LLM) sales agents in conversations with psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas over up to twenty turns. Unlike existing benchmarks that assume cooperative users, this benchmark challenges agents with resistance and includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products, and multiple price tiers. The study involved four controlled experiments with three iterations totaling 13,680 sessions, using retrieval-augmented generation for both agent and persona creation. Evaluation metrics cover primary outcomes, quality measures, and exploratory metrics, combining automated LLM-as-judge scoring with human assessments showing strong agreement and correlation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).

items.title: Researchers benchmark hyperbolic and Euclidean VAEs for unsupervised patent claim classification, finding hyperbolic models retrieve 52% more cross-category prior art on 45,000 US patents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Embedding Geometries and Clustering Algorithms for Unsupervised Patent Claim Classification
items.summary:
Researchers trained hyperbolic and Euclidean Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) on 45,000 US patents to evaluate unsupervised patent claim classification and prior-art retrieval. The hyperbolic model retrieved genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model, despite aligning less with official classification codes, highlighting different goals between classification and search needs.

The study also analyzed 10 technology domains with 50,000 additional patents, finding that a domain's classification breadth and patents per subgroup predict model performance. The researchers provide a 91-test automated implementation and report all findings with statistical transparency to guide practitioners on where the method is most valuable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior-art retrieval systems are structurally organized around classification codes, making cross-code discovery difficult. This paper asks if an unsupervised representation trained on patent text can recover relevant connections that code-restricted search cannot, and if hyperbolic space helps. We trained a hyperbolic and a matched Euclidean Variational Autoencoder (VAE) on 45,000 US patents (96 runs, 6 seeds). The hyperbolic model retrieves genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model (18.76% vs. 12.34% of top-10 results, 3,000 queries). This represents a practical gain for the motivating search problem. The hyperbolic model agrees less with official classification (NMI 0.2392 vs. 0.3206), which we explain geometrically: the two measures capture different goals, and only one aligns with prior-art search needs. In a study of 10 technology domains (50,000 more patents), we find that a domain's classification breadth--the number of distinct CPC subgroups spanned--predicts approach performance (Pearson r=-0.642, p=0.045, N=10), and that patents per subgroup is an even stronger predictor (r=0.715, p=0.020). This provides a checkable signal for practitioners to determine where the method is most valuable. We report all findings with statistical transparency and release a complete, 91-test automated implementation.

items.title: Researchers introduce a scalable method to maximize agent empowerment by increasing executable skills from a state, enabling emergent behaviors in complex environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Empowered Agents
items.summary: Researchers present a scalable approach to empowerment maximization, defining empowerment as the number of executable skills available from a given state. This method applies to various skill learning techniques and allows studying empowerment beyond simple tabular settings. Experiments demonstrate that maximizing empowerment leads to emergent behaviors such as resource gathering, environment modification, and survival strategies, including building structures in the Crafter environment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.

items.title: Researchers introduce EmbodiedCLBench, a benchmark for evaluating continual learning in self-evolving embodied agents using compositional generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark designed to assess continual learning capabilities in self-evolving embodied agents within simulated environments. The benchmark focuses on whether agents can learn basic tasks and recombine those skills to solve more complex, unseen tasks, highlighting the challenge of transferring experience in embodied settings.

Extensive experiments using EmbodiedCLBench revealed that while agents struggle with zero-shot performance on advanced tasks, prior experience with basic tasks consistently improves outcomes. However, this improvement does not scale with additional learning samples, indicating current agents have limited ability to extract meaningful information from increased experience. The benchmark aims to support the development of more effective continual learning methods for embodied agents, with code and datasets publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.

items.title: Researchers introduce ReTRAIL framework enabling long-horizon language model agents to rewind environment states while preserving learned knowledge to improve exploration and task solving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
items.summary:
Researchers present ReTRAIL, a framework designed for large language model agents operating in long-horizon environments where early errors can cause cascading failures. ReTRAIL allows agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while retaining knowledge from abandoned explorations, enabling better recovery and guidance for future decisions. The framework trains a shared policy using State-Anchored GRPO and a branch-advancement reward to improve execution and exploration progress.

Experiments on benchmarks including MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind function offers limited or negative effects, whereas ReTRAIL's combination of rewinding and experience reuse helps agents avoid unproductive states and leverage insights from previous attempts. This approach demonstrates the benefit of integrating environment rewinding with knowledge retention for solving complex, long-horizon tasks.
items.description:
Researchers present ReTRAIL, a framework designed for large language model agents operating in long-horizon environments where early errors can cause cascading failures. ReTRAIL allows agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while retaining knowledge from abandoned explorations, enabling better recovery and guidance for future decisions. The framework trains a shared policy using State-Anchored GRPO and a branch-advancement reward to improve execution and exploration progress.

Experiments on benchmarks including MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind function offers limited or negative effects, whereas ReTRAIL's combination of rewinding and experience reuse helps agents avoid unproductive states and leverage insights from previous attempts. This approach demonstrates the benefit of integrating environment rewinding with knowledge retention for solving complex, long-horizon tasks.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.

items.originalTitle: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
items.summary: Researchers introduce a black-box causal test to analyze object hallucination in large audio-language models (LALMs), isolating evidence regions via CLAP similarity and spectral gating across multiple models. They find that localization of evidence improves detection when controlling for duration, but detection effectiveness varies by model, with no unified causal-grounding profile transferable between models. The study also shows that combining contrastive decoding methods improves accuracy on Qwen2-Audio-7B from 57.1% to 71.9%, outperforming previous mitigation techniques. Source code and detailed findings are publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

items.title: KnowForge introduces role-specialized agents for open-domain multimodal document QA, improving F1 scores by up to 11 points on M3DocVQA and outperforming prior RAG models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA
items.summary:
KnowForge is a new pipeline for question answering over large, heterogeneous document collections that separates tasks among specialized agents: a Locator for searching, a Judge for bridging retrieval hops, a Deep Reader for reading text, images, and tables, and a synthesizer for answer formatting. Using a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model, KnowForge achieves an F1 score of 47.5 on the M3DocVQA benchmark, surpassing previous systems by significant margins and reaching 73.5 accuracy on MultiHop-RAG.
The system's design includes a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index and a typed evidence pool that merges search rankings. Ablation studies show the Deep Reader's contribution varies with the visual content of datasets, and combining agents into one reduces performance due to excessive searching. KnowForge's query latency depends on model calls rather than corpus size. The authors provide free access to the indexed benchmarks, along with all prompts and runner code for reproducibility.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval-augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open-domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one-shot retrieve-and-answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On MultiHop-RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single-document MMLongBench-Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT-4o reading page images (46.3). Per-job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round-budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read-only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask-ai/knowforge-bench

items.title: Researchers propose Foresight, an anticipatory generative model for road-network trajectories that improves next transition selection by incorporating future route anticipation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Looking Ahead and Back: Anticipatory Generative Modeling for Road-Network Trajectories
items.summary:
Trajectory generation is crucial for urban applications like traffic management and planning, but existing models often fail to accurately predict vehicle transitions at intersections, sometimes producing unrealistic paths off the road network. This paper introduces Anticipatory Generative Modeling, a new graph-constrained approach that models behavior on road networks by anticipating how future routes may unfold toward destinations. The proposed model, Foresight, uses a probabilistic "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop to enable longer-term foresight while generating sequential trajectories.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in trajectory generation tasks, addressing limitations of prior diffusion-based methods that simulate location sequences without effective next transition selection. This approach represents a shift from location simulation to behavior modeling, improving the realism and accuracy of generated vehicle trajectories within road networks.
