items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trajectory generation underpins urban applications such as traffic management and urban planning. Within road networks, vehicle movement along road segments is largely deterministic, whereas transitions at intersections are critical--multiple outgoing paths may appear equally plausible, yet they can lead to substantially different downstream routes. Existing generative methods such as diffusion models simulate location sequences and fail short of next transition selection, even producing trajectories that drift off the road network. To fill this gap, we advocate a fundamental shift: moving beyond location simulation toward behavior modeling on the road network. In this paper, we revisit trajectory generation through the lens of generative route planning, and introduce a new graph-constrained generative paradigm, Anticipatory Generative Modeling, which resolves next transition selection by incorporating the Anticipation of how the future route may unfold toward the destination. Concretely, we propose a novel generative model named Foresight that formulates a probabilistic model for an "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop that enables longer-term foresight while continuing sequential generation along the historical trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight wins state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: JANUS framework enhances long-horizon autonomous research by co-evolving world models to forecast outcomes and refine candidate selection, improving efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
items.summary:
JANUS is a new framework designed to accelerate long-horizon autonomous research by integrating future outcome forecasting with past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. It enables a research agent to propose candidates that the world model evaluates for value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility before execution, reducing costly trial-and-error feedback delays.

The system distills experience into evolving hierarchical skills for the research agent and exploration strategies for the world model, allowing continual co-evolution that sharpens candidate generation and predictive judgment over extended horizons. Evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks show JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both evolving efficiency and performance ceiling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.

items.title: BoundaryEvo introduces a two-stage data-model co-evolution framework to improve long-chain reasoning in small language models, adapting training data to evolving model capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BoundaryEvo: Data-Model Co-Evolution at the Capability Boundary for Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: BoundaryEvo proposes a novel approach to distilling long-chain reasoning from large teacher models to smaller language models by adapting training data as the student model's reasoning capability evolves. The framework includes Capability Priming, where a small set of teacher-generated reasoning trajectories are distilled without filtering, and Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution, which iteratively selects training examples that challenge but are solvable by the student model. Using only 1,000 training examples, BoundaryEvo significantly improves accuracy on 11 reasoning benchmarks, including raising Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 62.9 to 75.3 on IMO-AnswerBench and from 26.8 to 46.0 on AMO-Bench. The authors plan to release the code and data publicly.

Using only 1,000 training examples, BoundaryEvo significantly improves accuracy on 11 reasoning benchmarks, including raising Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 62.9 to 75.3 on IMO-AnswerBench and from 26.8 to 46.0 on AMO-Bench. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distilling long-chain reasoning trajectories from large teacher models provides an effective way to improve the reasoning ability of small language models. However, existing methods typically select a fixed training set before distillation, overlooking that the usefulness of a reasoning example changes as the student evolves. This mismatch becomes especially costly when only a small number of teacher trajectories can be used for training. Besides, examples already mastered provide little new supervision, while examples far beyond the capability of student may be difficult to learn from. Training data should therefore adapt as model capability evolves, yet reliable data selection is difficult when the student is initially weak. To address these challenges, our key idea is to first establish the basic reasoning capability and then adapt the training data to the evolving capability boundary of the student. We propose BoundaryEvo, a two-stage data--model co-evolution framework. In Capability Priming, we directly distill a small set of teacher-generated long reasoning trajectories without using a separate model to judge and filter them, allowing the student to acquire an initial reasoning capability before capability-aware data selection. In Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution, we repeatedly select questions that the current student has not mastered but the expert can reliably solve, and update the training data as the student evolves. items.summary: Researchers present ChemDiffAgent, a masked diffusion language agent designed to improve chemical reasoning by integrating external tools through iterative denoising and full-trajectory context. This approach addresses limitations of autoregressive models in bidirectional molecular understanding, coordinated tool planning, and multi-source evidence integration. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.

items.title: SqueezeBench launches a saturation-resilient benchmark for AI mathematical capability using machine-checked proofs and incremental record improvements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
items.summary:
SqueezeBench introduces a new benchmark designed to measure AI progress in mathematics without saturation by raising the difficulty bar with each success. It uses integer functions with known values for small inputs and maintains lower and upper bounds verified by machine-checked proofs in the Lean theorem prover. Submissions propose improved bounds that must be strictly better at some point, with proofs checked independently to ensure correctness and prevent trivial exhaustive searches.

The benchmark includes ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty initial records and tools for submission and verification. Baseline agents using a frontier language model improved every record with 82 accepted submissions, while newer models further improved 19 of 20 records with 60 additional accepted submissions. For most problems, some records remain asymptotically behind the best published bounds, indicating room for further AI-driven mathematical advances.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench, a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function $f(n)$ whose values are known only for small $n$, and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds $f$. A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds $f$, that it is no worse than the current record at any $n$, and that it is strictly better at some $n$. Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single $n$ or its growth rate. At every $n$, the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining $f(n)$. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes $f$ by exhaustive search at small $n$, and a maintainer only reads the submitter's report and looks for such a search at larger $n$. We release ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty proved initial records and the admission tools. As a baseline, agents based on a frontier language model, with at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, without going beyond the published literature. Agents based on two newer models then started from these records, had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.

items.title: Researchers introduce PRISM, a retrieval-augmented multimodal language model integrating heterogeneous clinical data for prognosis, achieving high AUROC scores on MDS-ED and external MC-MED benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
items.summary:
Researchers present PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model designed to integrate structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context for clinical prognosis. PRISM uses per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank that retrieves mean-pooled embeddings of similar patient encounters without including individual records in prompts. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieved AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality using a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to prior baselines.

Comparisons show PRISM outperforms a compact fusion model using the same evidence streams and frozen encoders, and replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization or removing pre-arrival history reduces performance. Genuine retrieval also outperforms random-neighbor retrieval, though statistical significance is marginal. On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning of PRISM reached 0.8611 AUROC, surpassing locally trained gradient boosting and source-only PRISM models. These results support the effectiveness of structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation for clinical prognosis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. Retrieval operates in representation space: the model receives mean-pooled embeddings of similar training-cohort encounters, while no individual retrieved record enters the prompt. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieves AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality. These results use a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to reported baselines. With benchmark-window inputs only, PRISM reaches 0.8895 AUROC, compared with 0.8937 for UniPACT and 0.8889 for MDS-ED. A matched-input compact fusion model using the same five evidence streams and frozen encoders reaches 0.7652 AUROC, versus 0.9092 for PRISM. Replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization reduces AUROC by 3.66 points; removing pre-arrival history reduces it by 1.97 points; and zeroing retrieval reduces it by 0.99 points. Genuine retrieval outperforms random-neighbor retrieval by 0.97 macro-average points, although a paired task-level sign test does not establish a uniform advantage (p=0.067). On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning reaches 0.8611 AUROC, compared with 0.8227 for locally trained gradient boosting and 0.7841 for source-only PRISM. These results support structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation.

We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.

items.title: Researchers propose PAGE framework using AI to analyze 3,929 American comics and 87 Japanese manga volumes, enabling large-scale study of visual and textual elements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
items.summary:
Researchers introduce PAGE, an AI-based framework that parses comic scans into panels, text, and bibliographic data, annotates pages with vision-language models, and grounds findings in human annotation to study comics at scale. They demonstrate PAGE on nearly 4,000 American comic books from 1938 to 1956 and 87 volumes of Japanese manga through three studies examining political power portrayal, visual style across artists, and speech patterns across traditions.

The framework aims to transform comics scholarship from isolated book studies to comprehensive archive analysis, offering tools to make comics searchable by content, accessible to blind and low-vision readers, and aiding preservation and artist crediting. The researchers outline a future research agenda where AI enhances the study, preservation, and accessibility of comics as a cultural medium.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.13840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.

items.title: Researchers propose IG-VLA framework for efficient vision-language-action reasoning by internalizing future scene imagination, achieving up to 6% success improvement and 6.38x speedup on robotic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
items.summary:
Researchers introduce IG-VLA, a vision-language-action reasoning framework that enables models to internally imagine future scene evolution in latent space, guiding robotic action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. The approach includes Scene Gist Memory, which compresses reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact token to reduce inference overhead.

Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench benchmarks show that IG-VLA's reasoning and gist policies outperform strong baselines by nearly 6% in success rate, with the gist policy achieving up to 6.38 times faster inference, reducing latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that internalized future spatiotemporal reasoning can improve both effectiveness and efficiency in robotic manipulation tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.02626v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

items.title: Researchers develop CircuitTree to compose multiple neural circuits into a syllable transcriber achieving 64.8% accuracy with shared components [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
items.summary: Researchers propose CircuitTree, a new method and data structure for composing many modular neural circuits into a single model, overcoming limitations of naive circuit union. They applied this to circuits pruned from HuBERT phoneme classifiers, combining 39 phoneme circuits into a syllable classifier that transcribes open syllables with 64.8% accuracy, close to a 66.0% ceiling without shared circuitry. The approach shares 99.5% of circuit components, demonstrating efficient hierarchical composition of interpretable subnetworks for speech tasks.
items.description: Researchers propose CircuitTree, a new method and data structure for composing many modular neural circuits into a single model, overcoming limitations of naive circuit union. They applied this to circuits pruned from HuBERT phoneme classifiers, combining 39 phoneme circuits into a syllable classifier that transcribes open syllables with 64.8% accuracy, close to a 66.0% ceiling without shared circuitry. The approach shares 99.5% of circuit components, demonstrating efficient hierarchical composition of interpretable subnetworks for speech tasks.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of circuit discovery is to decompose a monolithic neural network into tiny modular subnetworks which are interpretable in the sense that each does an identifiable subtask. We develop a practical method for composing arbitrarily many circuits into a single model. We propose a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm that overcomes limitations of previous attempts to compose circuits by naive union, then generalize it to $N$ circuits via CircuitTree, a new data structure built on a $\Theta(N\log N)$ tree-compose schedule. We compose circuits pruned from HuBERT for classifying individual phonemes into a syllable classifier, a capability none of the 39 phoneme circuits has individually. Chaining CircuitTrees into a hierarchy-of-circuits pipeline, we transcribe open syllables at 64.8\% accuracy, within 1.2 points of a 66.0\% ceiling that shares no circuitry at all, with 99.5\% of circuit components shared.

items.title: Researchers study self-preservation in language models using generated replay and task selection to reduce forgetting during continual learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Preservation in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers investigate how language models can preserve their capabilities during continual learning by generating replay data and selecting preservation tasks without access to original training data. They organize task descriptions into Task Banks to guide replay generation and test this approach on Qwen models of various sizes. The study finds that replay reduces forgetting beyond the tasks in the bank, combining partial banks improves retention, and models can help choose replay targets to enhance preservation, especially in larger models. The findings suggest that language models can support broader self-preservation by generating and selecting replay tasks, balancing preservation with learning new tasks under fixed example budgets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.

items.title: Researchers benchmark machine learning and time-series foundation models for day-ahead electricity forecasting in a university building, finding TimesFM 3.0 with covariates reduces mean absolute error by 43% compared to seasonal-naive methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Machine Learning and Time-Series Foundation Models for Day-Ahead Electricity Forecasting in a University Building
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural network, and pretrained TimesFM models for forecasting day-ahead electricity demand in a university building. They used chronological validation over 57 test days, comparing accuracy across workdays, weekends, and holidays, while considering local fitting and forecasting time. TimesFM 3.0 with weather covariates achieved the lowest overall errors, though XGBoost remained competitive without a clear advantage in mean absolute error. TimesFM performed well using only past electricity consumption, with covariates improving holiday forecasts but slightly worsening others. TimesFM requires no building-specific training, whereas XGBoost offers rapid local fitting and inference; an LSTM model took longer to train without outperforming these approaches.

Additional analyses revealed seasonal variation in electricity demand and showed that different weather data sources had minimal impact on TimesFM accuracy. The findings suggest pretrained TimesFM as a strong baseline for building electricity forecasting, with XGBoost as a viable locally fitted alternative. Incorporating covariates is particularly beneficial when improved holiday forecasts justify the extra input preparation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Day-ahead electricity forecasts can help building operators schedule heating, ventilation, and other services around anticipated demand. Choosing a forecasting model also requires balancing accuracy with its forecast-time inputs, local training, and computational requirements. We benchmark statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural-network, and pretrained TimesFM models for a university building. We use chronological validation and evaluate all configurations on the same 57 test days, comparing accuracy across workdays, weekends, and holidays alongside local fitting and forecasting time. Weather covariates use retrospective observations. TimesFM 3.0 with covariates achieves the lowest overall errors, reducing mean absolute error by approximately 43\% relative to weekly seasonal-naive forecasting. XGBoost remains competitive, although paired daily comparisons do not establish a clear mean-absolute-error advantage for TimesFM. TimesFM also performs strongly using only past electricity consumption. Adding covariates improves its holiday forecasts but slightly worsens workday and weekend forecasts, leaving overall mean absolute error almost unchanged. TimesFM requires no building-specific weight training, while XGBoost offers rapid local fitting and inference. The evaluated LSTM takes longer to fit without outperforming either approach. An exploratory historical evaluation reveals seasonal variation, while a separate weather-source comparison produces only small changes in the selected TimesFM configuration's accuracy. These results support pretrained TimesFM as a strong initial forecasting baseline for this building, with XGBoost as a competitive locally fitted alternative. Covariates are particularly useful when improved holiday forecasts justify the additional input preparation.

items.title: Researchers present Cancerous Backdoor Attack that gradually corrupts large language models' reasoning using invisible tokens and a stage controller [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
items.summary: Researchers introduce the Cancerous Backdoor Attack, a method that gradually corrupts reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through multiple stages using invisible tokens and a stage controller that tracks attack progression during inference. This approach contrasts with typical backdoor attacks that activate a single terminal behavior upon trigger satisfaction. The attack was evaluated across several reasoning datasets and consistently produced gradual reasoning corruption across different models and tasks. Compared to prior backdoor attack methods, Cancerous Backdoor Attack outperforms baselines and reveals that reasoning corruption can develop before becoming visible, indicating that answer accuracy alone may be insufficient for detecting such attacks.

The attack was evaluated across several reasoning datasets and consistently produced gradual reasoning corruption across different models and tasks. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.

items.title: Researchers propose Kronecker Product Attention for memory-efficient key-value cache compression in autoregressive models, achieving up to 10x reduction with maintained or improved accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kronecker Product Attention: Memory-Efficient KV Compression via Structured Factorization
items.summary: Researchers introduce Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), a method that compresses key and value activations in autoregressive generation models by representing them as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA generalizes previous approaches like Tensor Product Attention and incorporates a structured rotary embedding operator to preserve relative positional information without extra components. Empirical results show that KPA matches or outperforms existing attention mechanisms across multiple model scales and benchmarks while significantly reducing memory usage by up to tenfold. The approach includes a tunable hyperparameter allowing users to balance compression and accuracy without altering model architecture.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.

items.summary: GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their capability to identify necessary datasets, supporting resources, and constraints from natural language geo-analytic requests. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.

items.title: Researchers develop unsupervised multimodal reward model using a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone and perturbation-based training, outperforming GPT-4o on several benchmarks with minimal fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have created a vision-language reward model that requires no human preference labels by training a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone to score original web captions higher than perturbed versions. This approach, which uses perturbations instead of annotated preference pairs, achieves better or comparable performance to GPT-4o on three benchmarks, including a 6.6-point lead on VL-RewardBench, while using significantly less fine-tuning compute.

The model's success hinges on selecting the optimal intermediate layer, which improves performance by 5.8 points over the last layer. Training with perturbations yields 3 to 5 points more improvement than curated preference pairs, and retraining the head on verifier-labeled candidates reduces caption hallucination and improves image-generation pass rates. This method offers a cost-effective, annotator-free recipe for multimodal reward modeling that is defined by the training comparisons rather than benchmark rankings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.

items.title: Researchers introduce KITE, a knowledge-injected temporal encoder for forecasting rare events in multivariate time-series using semantic priors and switchable mechanisms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KITE: A Knowledge-Injected Temporal Encoder for Time-Series Event Forecasting
items.summary: Researchers present KITE, a self-supervised event forecaster that incorporates semantic priors—expert knowledge absent from scarce labels—into time-series forecasting through two switchable mechanisms: a covariate mechanism and an attention-bias mechanism. This approach improves prediction of rare, high-cost events by supplementing limited data with contextual knowledge without requiring per-dataset architecture changes. Experiments show that informative priors enhance in-domain forecasting accuracy and transfer effectively across domains, while priors redundant with observed data have no effect. KITE offers a flexible framework for contextual conditioning and aims to support scalable, cross-domain pretrained time-series models with explicit governing structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forecasting rare, high-cost events in multivariate time-series systems is hard because their precursors are seldom observed, so a purely data-driven model has little to learn from. The engineers who run these systems, however, hold knowledge that precedes such events, information absent from the scarce labels. We call this a semantic prior and inject it into a self-supervised event forecaster through two switchable mechanisms, a covariate mechanism and an attention-bias mechanism, each the identity at its null, so one architecture serves every prior type with no per-dataset architecture search. A prior helps when it supplies information the observed window does not already contain: in a short context an informative prior beats no prior in-domain (pooled h-AUROC over the no-prior baseline: a periodicity clock +14%, p<0.001; a conservation residual +47% at a 0.25 label fraction), and a working prior transfers out-of-domain (+53%), substituting for feature transfer, while priors the window already recovers stay inert and the attention-bias mechanism shows no measurable gain. KITE is a switchable, attributable route to contextual conditioning, and a substrate for scaling toward cross-domain, pretrained time-series foundation world models that carry their governing structure explicitly.

items.originalTitle: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
items.summary: Researchers address the challenge of predicting vehicle trajectories in urban roadway work zones by collecting WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset from 33 drivers using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with VR-controlled workers. Their proposed model, WZDrive, improves prediction accuracy by reducing key error metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The study fills a gap in autonomous driving research by combining human driving signals and multimodal learning to better handle the complexities of temporary lane changes and interactions in work zones.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.12747v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.

items.title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Generative Models Act as Simulators
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model can act as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. Plainly stated, our goal is to find a mapping between a generative model's latent state and the simulator state, where the model is trained on observations alone and the mapping is learned afterward. We test two kinds of mappings, both learned from observations paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even where steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, even though the state is decodable in every variant. In Othello, editability falls smoothly as the game is simplified, and even small rule changes have large consequences. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. A model can therefore be driven by a simulator it may have never learned.

items.title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.

items.title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.12957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.

items.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.

items.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13035v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.

items.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

items.title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP

Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. items.title: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative modeling for discrete data has been significantly advanced by learning continuous vector fields on the statistical manifolds to transport simple priors to target discrete distributions. However, because these continuous-time flows are not constrained to follow geodesics on the statistical manifold, thereby requiring multi-step numerical integration for simulation and leading to substantial computational costs during inference. In this work, drawing inspiration from the "straight and fast" properties of Rectified Flow in continuous Euclidean space, we propose the Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow) model, which enables one-step categorical generation on statistical manifolds by explicitly learning geodesic trajectories that adhere to the intrinsic Riemannian geometry. By rectifying the flow on the statistical manifold, we theoretically guarantee that trajectories between prior and target distributions approximate geodesics. This rectification significantly reduces the transport cost by aligning the learned trajectories directly along geodesics on the statistical manifold, allowing the model to map pure noise to target discrete data in a single step. Through extensive experiments on diverse real-world generative tasks, ranging from image and text to biological domains, we demonstrate ReSFlow's superior one-step generation quality, which truly embodies geodesically optimal and rapid categorical generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaohuanjia/ReSFlow.

items.title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.

items.title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM judges are increasingly deployed as panels, and disagreement among panel members is often read as a symptom of an unclear rubric. We test a label-free procedure that turns this disagreement into rubric repairs. The procedure decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested ones. An additional stage that moves text-checkable sub-criteria to deterministic checkers transferred none in our evaluation. Human labels are never used to select or edit clauses; they are used only to evaluate the outcome. We pre-specified four hypotheses in a version-controlled protocol and evaluated six rubric conditions with a panel of five judges from three providers on SummEval, the HealthBench meta-evaluation, and USR Topical-Chat, for a total of 129,770 judge requests, excluding retries. On SummEval, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's $\alpha$ by 0.069 (95% CI 0.046 to 0.092) over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that applied the same edits to an equal number of randomly chosen clauses that were not selected. Agreement with expert ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall $\tau$ difference -0.007, 95% CI -0.037 to 0.021). On HealthBench and USR, neither inter-judge agreement nor human agreement met the preregistered effect criteria. In a preregistered secondary comparison, human agreement after editing the contested clauses was lower than after editing the control clauses on all three datasets in point estimate, although no interval excluded zero. Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators. We will release code, frozen rubrics, item identifiers, and judge scores.

items.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.

items.title: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to build programs from scratch as software engineers do rather than to resolve issues within a repository or to generate a repository from a given requirements document. However, scalable verifiable training environments that force agents to discover what is required and to decide how the system should be designed remain scarce. Moreover, existing agent workflows also cannot sustain long-horizon development in which the agent explores the reference program before implementation. To address these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym, a framework consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env constructs verifiable training environments from repositories through a feedback-driven loop that repairs runtime sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests. Using this novel pipeline, we obtain 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust. Program-Agent combines a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review with revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. Experiments on ProgramBench show that both Program-Env and Program-Agent improve performance on program reproduction. Fine-tuning on trajectories with these constructed environments raises the performance of Qwen3.8-27B from 34.87% to 42.84%. Program-Agent further raises the base and SFT models to 55.71% and 56.25%, both exceeding some flagship models. We will release the ProgramGym to support further research on coding agents that build programs from scratch.

items.title: In-Context Learning for System Identification: Probabilistic Formulation, Long-Sequence Handling, and Benchmark Validation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: In-Context Learning for System Identification: Probabilistic Formulation, Long-Sequence Handling, and Benchmark Validation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional system identification typically involves two steps: initially, training data is processed to estimate a model of the system of interest; then, the model is used to predict outputs for new input queries. In contrast, recent in-context learning approaches learn a meta model that maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in a zero-shot fashion, bypassing explicit model estimation. This approach leverages a meta model trained offline, on large sets of synthetically generated data, to emulate the behavior of a system identification algorithm. In this work, we advance this meta-learning framework for system identification in three directions. First, we develop a unified probabilistic meta-identification architecture that combines a Transformer-based encoder-decoder with tailored mechanisms for handling long training sequences, enabling calibrated predictions over long horizons. Second, we show how a pre-trained meta model can act as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator for classical system identification, providing task-specific data that regularize parametric models when real data are scarce. Third, we systematically evaluate the framework on standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and on a challenging out-of-distribution scenario, demonstrating competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art methods and strong generalization, including cases where input-only adaptation is sufficient to handle significant distribution shifts.

items.title: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative Recommenders increasingly use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize outcomes that may appear hundreds or thousands of interactions after a decision. Standard RL propagates reward according to temporal proximity rather than explicit relevance, attenuating the signal assigned to distant but important actions and creating a source of sample inefficiency. We introduce Explanatory World Models (EWM), an attribution framework that uses explanations to identify the earlier events that plausibly contributed to a realized outcome. We instantiate EWM with a frontier language model and use its explanations as learning signals using a conservative hierarchical operator that recursively redistributes reward while preserving the undiscounted episode return. To investigate what constitutes a useful explanation, we operationalize three complementary variants inspired by Halpern's actual causation, Lombrozo's explanatory simplicity, and Deutsch's hard-to-vary explanations. We evaluate EWM on two controlled long-horizon RL benchmarks, a public sequential-recommendation benchmark, and an industry-scale generative recommender. On Crafter and WordCraft, EWM substantially outperforms PPO and LaRe, with its largest gains when rewards are most delayed. On KuaiRand, EWM outperforms SFT and LaRe offline and A2C online. Finally, in an offline evaluation of an industry generative recommender, EWM considerably improves Recall and increases behavioral proxies. These results suggest that explanations can provide structured and reusable credit for learning from delayed outcomes.

items.title: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13536v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a language model is distilled from a teacher that shares its base parameters, the student can inherit behavioural traits of the teacher---including misalignment---even from data that is semantically unrelated to the trait (Cloud et al., 2026). All existing defences require knowing the trait. We remove this requirement and prove that a subliminally transferred trait can be recovered from the parameter updates alone, without supervision, by exploiting a single asymmetry: the trait is expressed consistently across diverse datasets generated by the teacher, whereas task-specific and shared capabilities vary. The resulting estimator returns a weight-space direction that can be amplified to discover and interpret the trait or projected out to suppress it. Applied to the subliminal-learning benchmarks of (Cloud et al., 2026), our method recovers the transmitted animal-preference traits without any trait labels and suppresses their expression with almost no impact to task performance.

items.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.

items.title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.

items.title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.
